Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, I call to order the eighth meeting of the 63rd session of the Human Rights Council. We shall now continue the interactive dialogue with the Special Rapporteur on contemporary forms of slavery and trafficking in persons. According to our practice, we will start by hearing from the delegation of the country concerned by the report. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Brazil. You have five minutes. Ambassador, you have the floor.

Mr. Rapporteur, Thank you. Good to see you again. We appreciate the presentation of the report on the visit to Brazil in August 2025. Brazil reiterates its firm commitment to preventing and combating contemporary forms of slavery. We welcome the recognition of the significant progress achieved over the recent years, while acknowledging that challenges unfortunately remain. Contemporary forms of slavery are driven by a complex combination of socio-economic, historical and institutional factors, including social inequality, economic vulnerability and institutional shortcomings. Brazil has been making efforts across a wide range of areas to address the remaining gaps. Brazil has ratified all International Labor Organization instruments on forced labor, namely Convention 29 and its protocol, Convention 105 on abolition of forced labor, 138 on minimum wage, and 182 on worst forms of child labor. Our domestic legislation is robust, prohibiting contemporary forms of slavery child labor, and other forms of exploitation, including relevant provisions in the criminal code, the labor code, and the federal constitution. To advance eradication of situations in which persons are subject to conditions analogous to slavery, Brazil has implemented a comprehensive set of initiatives that constitute long-term state commitments, including the National Action Plan for the Eradication of Slave Labor, the National Plan to Combat Trafficking in Persons, and the National Plan for the Eradication of Child Labor. Coordinated strategies involving multiple government institutions have been established to conduct field operations, implement and implement legal measures. The Special Mobile Inspection Group is coordinated by the Ministry of Labor and includes the Labor Prosecution Office and the Federal Police. among other collaborating institutions. Since its creation in 1995, its operations have resulted in the rescue of approximately 68,000 workers. Children, people of African descent, indigenous peoples, quilombola communities, migrants, domestic workers, and sex workers face heightened risks of exploitation. These groups are affected by gender-based, racial, and other intersecting forms of discrimination and vulnerability, underscoring the importance to strengthen efforts aimed at their protection. Brazil has adopted the Statute of the Child and Adolescent, and more recently, the Digital Statute of the Child and Adolescent, which sets out provisions for the protection of children and young people in digital environments and establishes the national policy for the protection of the rights of children and young people in the digital environment. We would also like to highlight the EPE system, a free online platform designed to receive complaints and reports of child labor, including anonymous submissions. In addition, the Dial 100 hotline is available for filing complaints of human rights violations. Brazil has enacted robust legislation for the protection of domestic workers, which has contributed to addressing their social vulnerability by reducing formality and recognizing their entitlement to labor rights and social protection. The legislation and policies in force in this area are consistent with ILO Convention 189, which Brazil has ratified. This legal framework, combined with broader measures prohibiting forced labour, has contributed to reducing cases of domestic servitude and improving working conditions for domestic workers. The report refers to the protection of victims, a key component of our strategy to eradicate forced labour. The rescue of workers subjected to degrading conditions is part of a comprehensive process that requires specialized assistance to facilitate their reintegration into society. Such assistance is provided for under the National Protocol for Assistance to Victims of Slave Labor. Mr. Rapporteur, Brazil takes note of the report and its conclusions and recommendations. We remain committed to considering the issues raised and further strengthening the mechanisms in place to combat contemporary forms of slavery as a matter of state priority with a view to addressing the remaining gaps. I thank you. I thank you, Mr. Chair.

Muchas gracias.

Thank you. I now invite interested delegations to ask questions to the special rapporteur and to make comments on his report. Speaking time is one minute 30 seconds for all. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Belgium on behalf of a group of countries.

Mr. Vice-President, I have the honour to speak on behalf of the Benelux countries. We align ourselves with the EU statement and thank the Special Rapporteur for her report and the vision for the merged mandate she outlines therein. Madam Special Rapporteur, as your report points out, contemporary slavery and trafficking in persons unfortunately remain widespread. While they can take many different forms and occur in all regions of the world, it is undeniable that they primarily affect those most vulnerable worldwide, particularly women and girls. In this regard, we welcome that you chose to adopt an intersectional perspective as a priority throughout all your activities. Taking into account the multiple and intersecting forms of discrimination is crucial to understanding the dynamics of slavery and trafficking. As you also mentioned, a multi-stakeholder approach is essential to address these complex and multifaceted issues comprehensively. Civil society, the private sector, states and intergovernmental organizations must work hand in hand to eliminate slavery and trafficking. The Benelux countries remain fully committed to putting an end to these scourges, while offering redress to victims and survivors and holding perpetrators accountable. Special Rapporteur, can you share some good legislative practices as regards protection for victims and survivors of slavery and trafficking? I thank you. Thank you very much.
I give the floor to the distinguished representative of the European Union.

Vice President, the EU thanks the Special Rapporteur for the report. We welcome your vision for the joint slavery and trafficking mandate, showing the advantages of this holistic approach. Trafficking in persons and contemporary forms of slavery entail some of the gravest violations of human rights of our time. The EU has taken legislative steps to address this and stands ready to work with you in strengthening the implementation of anti-slavery and anti-trafficking frameworks and close protection and accountability gaps and ensuring human rights-based, survivor-centered, gender-responsive and child-sensitive response. Two years ago, the EU adopted a revised anti-trafficking directive. For the first time, it makes it mandatory for EU member states to criminalize the knowing use of services provided by trafficked persons, and it explicitly includes the exploitation of forced marriage, illegal adoption, and surrogacy. Beyond criminal law, the EU has moved to close the market for forced labor itself. The forced labor regulation prohibits products made with forced labor anywhere in the world from entering the EU market, with the possibility that affected workers be compensated before such products can circulate again. Madam Special Rapporteur, in what areas do you perceive the biggest protection and accountability gaps? I thank you.

Muchas gracias.

Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Thailand on behalf of a group of countries.

Thank you, Mr. Vice President. Thailand has the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of a cross-regional group of over 40 countries. We are deeply alarmed by the evolving and industrial scale of online scams and its human rights impacts. At least 300,000 people from 80 countries work in scam compounds. Many are subjected to confinement, trafficking for forced criminality, physical and sexual violence, torture, and other serious human rights violations. As the High Commissioner underscored, online scams have become a disturbing new form of contemporary slavery and human trafficking. Scam networks are expanding globally, linking forced labor, trafficking in persons, and transnational organized crime. They exploit digital technologies, benefit from corruption, and gaps in the rule of law and across jurisdictions to sustain and expand their operations. Addressing this crisis requires a global response rooted in human rights, while applying a victim-centered approach and the principle of non-punishment for unlawful acts committed as a direct consequence of being trafficked. We call for enhanced cooperation to promote prevention, prosecute criminal networks, combat corruption, disrupt illicit financial flows, strengthen victims' protection, and ensure accountability.

I thank you.

Thank you very much.

I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Kenya on behalf of the African Group.

Mr. Vice President, the African Group thanks the Special Rapporteur for her report, which highlights the persistence of modern forms of slavery and human trafficking, as well as the new dynamics that continue to fuel these serious human rights violations. The African Group shares its concerns regarding the many factors of vulnerability that contribute to the exploitation of people, in particular poverty, inequality, conflict, forced displacement and precarious migration situations. It also notes its concern that persons in vulnerable situations, especially those of African descent, remain particularly exposed to various forms of exploitation and abuse. Africa remains fully committed in the fight against these problems. In this regard, the continent has had since 2021 the African Union policy on the prevention of human trafficking, which constitutes an important framework for strengthening victim protection, the cooperation between states and the fight against criminal networks involved in trafficking. The Afghan Group emphasizes, however, that the scale and the transnational nature of these phenomena requires enhanced international cooperation, particularly at cross-border, regional and interregional levels. Such cooperation must make it possible to dismantle criminal networks more effectively, strengthen mechanisms for identifying and protecting victims, and ensure that the perpetrators are brought to justice. A full copy of the statement shall be posted on the Extranet. Thank you.

Thank you very much.

I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Nigeria, on behalf of a group of countries.

Thank you, Mr. Vice President. I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of a group of ECOWAS states, namely Benin, Gambia, Ghana, and my own country, Nigeria. We welcome the Special Rapporteur and congratulate her on assuming the newly merged mandate on contemporary forms of slavery and trafficking in persons. The ECOWAS region continues to face trafficking and exploitation in contexts shaped by poverty, inequality, climate pressures, displacement, and migration. We therefore welcome the report's emphasis on prevention and on addressing the structural drivers of vulnerability. For ECOWAS states, mobility remains central to livelihoods, regional integration, and economic opportunity. Our framework on free movement reflects this reality. Legitimate mobility must therefore be facilitated while trafficking, forced labor, and abusive recruitment are effectively prevented and addressed. Member states are strengthening bilateral and subregional cooperation through memorandum of understanding, information sharing, victim referral, safe return, and reintegration. We are also implementing the ECOWAS Labor Migration Strategy and Action Plan 2025 to 2035 and advancing common approaches to bilateral labor migration agreements and fair recruitment with the aim of improving worker protection and expanding safer migration pathways. We encourage the United Nations system and relevant partners to deepen cooperation with COAS and its member states, particularly on cross-border referral, fair recruitment, data sharing, victim protection, investigation, and prevention. I thank you, Mr. Vice President.

Muchas gracias.

Thank you very much. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Germany.

Thank you, Mr. President. We align ourselves with the EU statement and thank the Special Rapporteur for her report. We welcome her vision for the newly merged mandate and appreciate the holistic approach that it enables. Aside from efficiency gains, this was a key consideration for Germany as a member of the core group when we merged the mandate. As you point out, Madam Special Rapporteur, the issues are as relevant as ever. Human beings continue to be bought, sold, traded, exploited, trafficked, and thereby treated as if they were property. These crimes are truly global in nature and can only be effectively addressed through close cooperation among the international community. Combating criminal networks and holding perpetrators accountable is a key priority for Germany. In this context, we also welcome the mandate's focus on new and emerging technologies and their underlying opportunities and risks. We join the Special Rapporteur's call for more effective cooperation, coordination, and collaboration of all stakeholders. A human rights-based and survivor-centered approach is essential, one of the reasons why Germany consistently supports the Voluntary Trust Fund on Contemporary Forms of Slavery. Let me close by wishing you, Madame Special Rapporteur, success in your new mandate and calling on all to cooperate fully with you.

Thank you.

Thank you very much. The list of speakers is now closed. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Thailand.

Mr. Vice President, Thailand thanks the Special Rapporteur for her report. Scam operations involve global networks of transnational crime that violate human rights, Since February 2025, Thailand, in collaboration with partners, has assisted in repatriating more than 13,000 people from over 40 countries rescued from scam centers in our neighboring country. Combating human trafficking and online scams is therefore high on Thailand's national agenda. Our anti-trafficking efforts are guided by domestic laws, particularly the Anti-Trafficking in Persons Act and the Labor Protection Act, regularly revised to respond to the evolving nature of these crimes. Since 2022, Thailand has put in place the national referral mechanism to provide assistance to victims in accordance with trauma-informed, victim-centered approaches and a non-punishment principle, through screening, victim identification, and protection. Our effort to combat trafficking for forced criminality is based on whole-of-government and whole-of-society approaches. Standard operating procedures are being drafted, and an operational task force has been established. We will continue working with partners to eradicate online scams and protect victims of trafficking for forced criminality. We thank all participants for joining our side event this afternoon on trafficking in persons in the context of online scams earlier. Thank you very much.

Thank you very much.

I give the floor to the distinguished representative of UNDP.

Thank you. UNDP welcomes the Special Rapporteur's report. We support her emphasis on prevention and on the structural drivers of slavery and trafficking. Modern slavery and human trafficking affect over 50 million people worldwide and generate more than $236 billion in illicit profits each year. Those profits move through the global financial system. We share the Special Rapporteur's concern that business can create conditions in which exploitation thrives, particularly where oversight and accountability remain weak, and that new technologies are complicating financial tracing. The financial sector has an important role in prevention. Through responsible investment, humanized due diligence, risk disclosure, and survivor-centered financial inclusion, financial institutions can address risks across value chains. Through UNDP's Finance Against Slavery and Trafficking Initiative, with the support of Liechtenstein, we work with governments, financial institutions, and survivors to put that role in practice. We welcome the recognition that global markets, trade, and financial flows are expanding domains for anti-slavery action, and the caution that the economic case must not displace a rights-based approach. Madam Special Rapporteur, how can survivor expertise be embedded in financial sector prevention from the outset?

And what would you ask of states and financial institutions to make that happen? Thank you.
Thank you very much. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Philippines.

Thank you, Mr. Vice President. The Philippines warmly congratulates Ms. Katharina Schwars on her appointment and welcomes her inaugural report. The merged mandate brings together two separate but interconnected issues, enabling a more coherent and comprehensive human rights response. We appreciate the Special Rapporteur's intersectional lens and its emphasis on prevention, structural drivers, and a whole systems approach. As a country committed to the protection of all persons in situations of vulnerability, including migrants, we support the attention given to the migration and trafficking nexus. We stress the imperative to safeguard the rights and welfare of all migrant workers all throughout the migration cycle. We likewise agree that climate change and environmental degradation are threat multipliers, heightening risk to trafficking, forced labor, sexual exploitation, and other abuses, especially of women and girls. The focus on technology facilitated trafficking and the urgent need for robust, multilateral collaboration to combat online scam hubs, digital recruitment, and other forms of exploitation online is most welcome. The Philippines is ready to support the special rapporteur and wishes her every success in her important work.

Thank you.

Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Republic of Korea.

Thank you, Mr. Vice President. The Republic of Korea warmly congratulates Ms. Katerina Sarantopoulou on her appointment as the Special Rapporteur on contemporary forms of slavery and trafficking in persons and welcomes her inaugural report. We take particular note of her identification of survivor participation and leadership and domestic legislation as priorities in carrying out her new merged mandate. My delegation wishes to take this opportunity to emphasize the importance of addressing technology-facilitated trafficking in persons. In particular, first, online scamming is an emerging and deeply concerning form of exploitation in which trafficked persons are coerced into conducting online fraud and cyber-enabled criminal activities. The Republic of Korea has been actively engaged in advancing this agenda. In March this year, we co-hosted an HRC side event titled "Human Rights Impact of Online Scams" with OCHR. In June, we launched the Group of Friends for Combating Technology-Facilitated Trafficking in Persons in New York, which currently comprises 28 participating countries. We also co-sponsored the HRC side event on online scams with a particular focus on jurisdictional gaps, hosted by Thailand earlier today. Finally, we share the Special Rapporteur's observation in her report that technological advances are seen as a double-edged sword. We hope she will continue to pay close attention to technology-facilitated trafficking in persons, including by exploring ways to harness emerging technologies, such as AI, in our response. I thank you.
Thank you very much. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Costa Rica.

Thank you, Vice President. Costa Rica welcomes the report by the special rapporteur, and we share concern about the growing convergence of crises that worsen the vulnerability to human trafficking, especially mixed and irregular migratory flows. As a country of origin, transit and destination, we directly face the risks that the rapporteur describes, including the use of irregular migration a tool for coercion, the precarity generated by increasingly restrictive migratory routes and the disproportionate impact on women, children, indigenous people and migrants. We fully agree with the need for an approach focused on prevention and on structural factors, as well as bolstering regional cooperation in the face of phenomena that transcend borders. Costa Rica has its law 9095 and its national coalition against human trafficking and illicit traffic in migrants, and it together with UNODC, the IMO and UN Women, a joint programme against human trafficking, which recently created a digital dashboard for monitoring administrative data, which is presented to the regional coalition against human trafficking and illicit migrant trafficking. We reiterate our willingness to share our experiences with other states. And we ask the rapporteur, what specific recommendations can you propose so that migratory governance strengthens rather than weaken, uh, protection responses in the face of trafficking? Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Holy See.

Thank you, Mr. Vice President.

My delegation. takes note of the Special Rapporteur's first report. Slavery and trafficking are complex issues with many facets. Both are driven by the commodification and exploitation of the human person. Regrettably, traditional forms of slavery have not been fully eradicated, and new forms of exploitation and trafficking continue to emerge. As such, they must be firmly condemned in all their forms.

New forms of slavery are fueled by economic chains and digital infrastructures. Supply chains, therefore, must be more transparent to prevent hidden exploitation.

Companies and investors must

adopt clear criteria for ethical verification, placing worker protection, combating forced labor, and assessing social impact of business models as their top priorities. Digital platforms must cooperate with authorities and civil society to prevent communication, payment, and profiling tools from being used to recruit and control victims. When these efforts converge, the digital environment can be transformed

into a space of protection, prevention, and human dignity.

As Pope Leo XIV observes, criminal networks use online platforms, messaging systems, anonymous payment methods, and profiling techniques in order to recruit, control, and transform victims of trafficking, very often minors. Indeed, the fight against new forms of slavery is a decisive test for the ethical discernment of AI.

Thank you, Mr. Chair.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Benin.

Thank you, Vice-President. Benin aligns with the statement by the African Group and the ECOWAS States. We congratulate the Special Rapporteur for submitting her first report in the context of the merger of mandates as per resolution 6025 of the Council. We welcome, with a view to having a comprehensive approach to fighting contemporary forms of slavery and human trafficking, my country remaining profoundly concerned by the persistence of phenomena that constitute grave human rights violations and disproportionately impact women, children and people in situations of vulnerability. Given those challenges, my country continues to bolster its own institutional legal framework, implementing specific protection mechanisms for children, women and other vulnerable people, as well as promoting enhanced regional co-operation in the framework of ECOWAS. We foster a comprehensive approach based on human rights that combines prevention, outreach, protection and care for victims. prosecution of perpetrators and bolstering regional and international co-operation. In view of the recommendations and findings in your report, what international and regional cooperation mechanisms could be further consolidated to improve identification, protection and charge for the victims of human trafficking, especially in situations of cross-border trafficking involving women and children. Thank you.
I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Jordan.

Thank you, Vice-President. We thank the Special Rapporteur, Madame Schwitz, for her new mandate. We wish her every success and we thank her for the report. Exploitation begins with the promise of work and ends with denial of freedom. Technology is used to lure victims, so the means of perpetrating the crime have developed, and we need to develop means to combat that crime. That is why the new mandate is important. Jordan contributed to developing the resolution that established it. We agree with the rapporteur that the merger is important to improve co-ordination of efforts to fight slavery and human trafficking. What is particularly important is organised migration and bolstering international co-operation. We need to be able to implement the recommendations, since they improve national legislation and practices. We would like to know from the rapporteur what role the new mandate can play in order to implement the past recommendations and support states in in the process of implementation. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Ethiopia.

Thank you, Mr. Vice President. Ethiopia welcomes the report of the Special Rapporteur, and we share the concern that conflict, poverty, displacement, climate-related challenges, and irregular migration can heighten vulnerability to exploitation and trafficking. These interconnected challenges require comprehensive, nationally owned and context sensitive responses supported by genuine international cooperation and capacity building. Ethiopia continues to strengthen its legal, institutional and policy frameworks to prevent trafficking and protect vulnerable persons while addressing its root causes through inclusive development, expanded social protection, employment opportunities and strengthened access to justice. We underscore that combating slavery and trafficking requires enhanced international and regional cooperation, particularly in addressing transnational criminal networks, protecting victims, promoting safe migration, and strengthening law enforcement and judicial capacities. We also recognize the important role of responsible business practices, civil society, and affected communities in prevention and protection efforts. International cooperation should, however, respect national ownership, sovereignty, and the diverse circumstances and capacities of states. In closing, Ethiopia calls upon the international community to strengthen cooperation, coordination, and collective action to combat contemporary forms of slavery and trafficking in persons, and reaffirms its commitment to actively contribute to this shared effort. I thank you.

Muchas gracias.

Thank you very much. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Iceland on behalf of a group of countries.

Mr. Vice President, I have the honor to speak on behalf of the Nordic-Baltic states. We welcome the establishment of this mandate, combining two previous and interlinked mandates into one, and thank the Special Rapporteur for her latest report to the Council, which provides important insights into contemporary forms of slavery and trafficking. The fight against trafficking and contemporary forms of slavery requires a global response. We continue to advocate for a coherent, multidimensional, and multi-action across all levels. While we recognize the progress and the hard-won gains, including the promising efforts to combating slavery and trafficking in value chains, The rising tide of interconnected global challenges that contribute to contemporary slavery and trafficking are concerning, including conflict, climate change, displacement and rapid developments in emerging technologies. It is becoming increasingly clear that the digital environment and its transnational nature present new challenges in the fight against contemporary forms of slavery and trafficking in persons. At the same time, digital technologies can strengthen prevention and detection of these violations. Madam Special Rapporteur, what are the most important factors that States should consider when regulating their digital environment with the aim of preventing and combating contemporary forms of slavery and trafficking in persons? I thank you.

Muchas gracias.

Thank you very much. I now call upon the distinguished representative of Togo.

President, the Togolese delegation thanks the Special Rapporteur for his report. which particularly highlights contemporary challenges in combating slavery and human trafficking in their various forms, and also highlights aggravating factors such as poverty, climate change, and the weak regulation of economic and migration circuits, as well as emerging technologies. Togo is fully mindful of the devastating impacts of this scourge, and it has taken measures to strengthen its national legislation and its institutional framework, particularly when it comes to persons and the family, the school environment, the learning environment and the workforce. Follow-up is guaranteed by the National Commission to Combat Human Trafficking, which was set up in February 2023. President, despite the headway made, challenges remain. That is why, in a spirit of ongoing improvement, the Togolese Government intends to further bolster prevention and the early detection of cases of trafficking, with a view to affording better protection to victims. With this in mind, the delegation of Togo would like to call for a strengthening of cross-border, regional and international cooperation so as to dismantle criminal networks who feed off human trafficking. I thank you.
Thank you very much. I'd now like to give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

Vice-President, my delegation thanks the Special Rapporteur for presenting the report and associates with the statements made by Kenya on behalf of the African Group. The DRC hails the implementation of resolution 65 of 8 October 2025. The merging of mandates on contemporary forms of slavery and human trafficking is a strategic major headway and streamlines our efforts and overcomes institutional barriers to better target the profound causes of these interconnected scourges. My country fully aligns with the threats and challenges highlighted in the report. In the face of criminal networks that exploit the vulnerability of women and children, the DRC has stepped up its national fight, particularly by strengthening its national legislation and its victim protection mechanisms. However, we would underscore that the effectiveness of the new mandate will depend on a holistic approach. It is vital to incorporate the impact of climate change, poverty and armed conflicts. which act as multiplying risks for modern slavery and human trafficking. The DRC would like to reassure the Special Rapporteur of its full cooperation in implementing the priorities. We call upon the international community to increase technical and financial support to states affected to transform the guidance into specific actions on the ground. I thank you.
Thank you very much. I'd like to give the floor to the distinguished representative of Cote d'Ivoire.

Vice-President, Cote d'Ivoire would like to align with the statements to which it belongs to and would like to thank the Special Rapporteur for the report on the current status, the challenges and priorities in combating contemporary forms of slavery and human trafficking. My country regrets the fact that slavery and human trafficking persist endemically in all regions of the world. aggravated by converging crises, climate, conflict, poverty, migration, inequalities and structural factors. Furthermore, despite legislative headway made and international efforts, serious shortcomings remain in the prevention, protection of victims, access to justice and holding the perpetrators responsible, particularly in the private sector. For its part, the Government of Cote d'Ivoire amongst other actions, conducted an awareness-raising campaign in 2025 in cocoa-producing rural areas, combining radio messages, community workshops and the distribution of educational support. This initiative has made it possible to inform thousands of families about the dangers of child labour and to encourage schooling. In parallel to this, welcome centres were opened to support children withdrawn from forced labour, providing them with schooling and psychosocial follow-up. Field actions are added to strengthened legal arsenal and a robust institutional framework. By way of conclusion, we remain convinced that by collective action alone, which is coordinated and based on human rights, will it be possible to definitively eradicate all forms of slavery and human trafficking.

I thank you.

Thank you. I call upon the distinguished representative of Zambia.

Mr. Vice President, Zambia welcomes the special rapporteur and the opportunity presented by the new integrated mandate to strengthen global action against contemporary forms of slavery and trafficking in persons. Zambia's experience as a country of origin, transit, and destination demonstrates that trafficking and exploitation cannot be addressed through criminal justice measures alone. We have strengthened our legal framework, including through amendments to the Anti-Human Trafficking Act. Equally important, however, is addressing vulnerability before exploitation occurs. Poverty, informality, unemployment, and unsafe migration can expose individuals to deceptive recruitment and exploitation. Zambia, therefore, regards expanded access to free education, skills development, social protection, and economic empowerment of women and youth as part of prevention. As a land-linked country sharing borders with eight neighbors, Zambia particularly recognizes that trafficking networks do not respect national borders. Effective responses require regional cooperation, information sharing, safe migration, and stronger protection through recruitment and labor supply chains. I thank you.
Thank you very much. I'd like to call upon the distinguished representative of Cambodia.

Mr. Vice President, contemporary forms of slavery and trafficking in persons are transnational challenges that recognize no national boundaries. No country, regardless of its size, wealth, or power, can address them alone. Cooperation is therefore a practical necessity. We have consistently implemented measures to combat transnational crime through our relevant laws and national strategic plan. Our authorities have dismantled criminal networks, rescued thousands of victims, and arrested perpetrators. In partnership with UNODC, Interpol, and the Lancang Mekong Integrated Law Enforcement and Security Cooperation Center, Cambodia will host international conference on combating online scam in Phnom Penh on 23, 24 September, contributing to collective action against this global threat. Cambodia welcome close cooperation and collective action to combat international crimes and reaffirms that all measures to combat such crime must be grounded in international law. Any attempt by a neighboring country to combat online scam must not be misused as a pretext to justify action that violate the sovereignty and territorial integrity of state, contrary to the purpose and principle of the United Nations Charter. I thank you.

Muchas gracias.

Thank you very much. I call upon the distinguished representative of the Sovereign Order of Malta.

Excellencies, the Sovereign Order of Malta thanks the Special Rapporteur, Professor Katerina Schwarcz, for her excellent report. Theodor Molta expresses a deep concern about the current situation regarding human trafficking. Today, the number of people living in conditions of slavery is higher than at any time in history. This situation requires urgent and coordinated action by the international community to protect the victims. We welcome the priorities the Special Rapporteur has given to the participation and leadership of survivors and her intersectional survivor-centered approach to addressing structural drivers of vulnerability, such as poverty, conflict, displacement,

and discrimination.

The Sovereign Order of Malta remains firmly committed to combat slavery and trafficking in persons. For the 25th anniversary of the Palermo Protocol, Theodor Molta organized in Rome a conference on human trafficking focused on concrete prevention measures and efforts needed worldwide to combat modern slavery. In addition, this year, we are preparing with the San Remo Institute a series of online courses to help close this training gap, offering accessible and practical learning tools. Thank you, Mr. President.
Thank you very much. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Angola.

Mr. Vice President, Angola welcomes the Special Rapporteur's report and reaffirms its commitment to fighting contemporary forms of slavery and trafficking persons, which are serious violations of human dignity. In Africa, poverty, inequality, irregular migration, and limited economic opportunities create vulnerabilities that are exploited by transnational criminal networks. We are particularly concerned about forced criminality, where victims are forced to commit crimes through threats, violence, or abuse. Angola has strengthened its legal and institutional response to trafficking, with strong focus on prevention, protection of victims, and accountability of perpetrators. Victims must remain at the center of our response. Women and children are particularly vulnerable, and people forced to commit unlawful acts as a result of exploitation should be recognized and treated first and foremost as victims and rights holders. No country can tackle these transnational crimes alone. Stronger cross-border cooperation, information sharing, capacity building, and support for victims reintegration are therefore essential. Special rapporteur, what practical measures would you recommend to strengthen the cooperation with African states to dismantle trafficking networks while ensuring effective protection for victims or forced criminality?

Thank you.

Thank you. I give the floor to the Senior Representative of Malawi.

Thank you, Mr. Vice President. Malawi thanks the Special Rapporteur on contemporary forms of slavery and trafficking in persons for her report, which provides a review of current threats and opportunities in the anti-slavery and anti-trafficking landscape, and outlines the priorities that she will focus on during her tenure in the new merged mandate. Malawi concurs with the report's findings that whilst the fight against contemporary forms of slavery and trafficking in persons is facing a uniquely challenging landscape that poses significant threats to progress, there are key strategies that states can implement for the effective elimination of exploitation and trafficking. To deal with the challenge of multidimensional poverty and inequality, which the report cites as the most decisive driver for slavery and trafficking, Malawi is implementing the Malawi Vision 2063 plan. The plan aims to transform Malawi into an inclusively wealthy, self-reliant, and industrialized upper-middle income country by 2063. Malawi commends the Special Rapporteur for advancing the critical importance of an intersectional perspective in her tenure. In conclusion, Malawi would like to pose a question to the Special Rapporteur: What concrete steps can national mechanisms take...
Thank you very much. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Yemen, a video statement.

President, we would like to thank the Special Rapporteur for her efforts, and we firmly condemn all forms of slavery and forced labour, as well as trafficking in persons. We are majorly concerned about the serious and systematic violations which are perpetrated by the militia. in the areas under their control, in particular forced recruitment and the exploitation of thousands of children in absurd wars that are being waged. Added to this, we have exploitation and the trafficking of migrants and refugees. They are called upon to take part of serious human violations of international law and the international community is tasked with combating these crimes and aligning its national legislation with international norms. We are determined to protect those most in need. We call upon the international community and the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights to provide technical assistance and to bolster the abilities of national authorities and agents tasked with implementing laws so as to combat networks by ensuring accountability at the same time. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the Turkish representative of the Council of Europe.

Development imposed without consent violates human dignity and undermines trust. Authentic participation ensures accountability, equity, and sustainability. Communities must have access to information, freedom of expression, and genuine opportunities to influence decisions that affect their lives and environments. When participation is inclusive, especially of women, youth, indigenous people, and persons with disabilities.
Thank you. I give the floor to Right Livelihood Award Foundation.

Mr. President, Right Livelihood welcomes the Special Rapporteurs and its recognition that the right to development requires active, free and meaningful participation. Participation is not meaningful when communities are consulted only after fundamental decisions have already been made. The experience of Right Livelihood laureates across the world demonstrate what is at stake. In the context of extractive and large-scale development projects, indigenous people and local communities continue to face dispossession from their lands, destruction of livelihoods and ecosystems, forced displacement, and threats to their cultural and spiritual heritage. These are not merely shortcomings in consultation. They represent a fundamental failure to put people at the center of development. States must guarantee meaningful and effective participation through the entire project lifecycle prior and informed consent as required under international human rights law. Companies also have responsibility to respect human rights. Neither state authorization nor investment interest can justify proceeding with projects while serious human rights and environmental impacts remain unaddressed. As the Special Rapporteur rightly emphasizes, communities must be able to shape both the process and its outcome, including the possibility to say no to a proposed project. We therefore ask the Special Rapporteur what recourse is available to communities when states and companies restrict or deny meaningful participation and choose to pursue their own interests despite community opposition, serious human rights concerns and environmental harm. Thank you.

Muchas gracias.

Mr. President, Mr. Rapporteur, between 1904 and 1908, German colonial troops systematically executed and starved thousands of Herero and Nama men, women and children in Namibia. Until today, the genocide has caused irreparable damage and transgenerational harm for their descendants. Over 100 years later, the Ovaherero and Nama are still prevented from accessing some of their ancestral land and cultural heritage sites. We welcome the recommendation to Germany to offer an unconditional apology for the genocide against the Ovaherero and Nama peoples and to to return all human remains and artifacts of indigenous peoples displayed in German museums, universities, and private collections as a matter of urgency. Amnesty International shares the Special Rapporteur's concerns that, despite pledging funds for reconstruction and development programs in Namibia, German authorities continue to deny any legal obligation to provide reparations for the colonial crimes committed by German forces. Development aid is not a substitute for full and effective reparation. As several UN experts have warned, development aid risks perpetuating rather than disrupting colonial dynamics. We also echo the Special Rapporteur's concerns regarding the lack of meaningful participation of the Ovaherero and Nama peoples in the negotiations between the governments of Germany and Namibia. There cannot be true justice if those affected are excluded from the talks. The German government must guarantee the full, effective and meaningful participation of affected groups in any reparations negotiations. Thank you.
